healthInfo.healthcareSystem: Universal (Protection Maladie Universelle / PUMA, formerly Sécurité Sociale)
healthInfo.qualityNotes: World-class healthcare system with excellent hospitals and specialists. English is commonly spoken in medical settings in Paris and major cities, less so in rural areas. Reimbursement through French social security requires EU citizenship or a European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) for EU residents.
healthInfo.pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-8pm weekdays, reduced hours on weekends. Some pharmacies in large cities are open 24/7. Look for the green cross sign.
healthInfo.pharmacyTips: Pharmacies (pharmacie) are widely available. Many medications require a prescription. Some OTC items like basic painkillers, antiseptics, and eye drops are available without prescription. Pharmacists are knowledgeable and can advise on minor ailments.
healthInfo.prescriptionRules: EU/Schengen prescriptions are accepted in France. Non-EU prescriptions require a French doctor's consultation. Many common medications in the US require prescriptions here.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products require a prescription in France. Some codeine products are available behind the pharmacy counter.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A Schengen prescription or French doctor's prescription is required. Some ADHD medications are not available in France.

restrictedMeds.name: Sleeping pills (benzodiazepines)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require a prescription. France has strict guidelines around their use.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis was legalized in France in 2021 but remains very restricted and only available through specific channels for a limited number of conditions.

healthInfo.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter and prescription (ideally in French or English) for all prescription medications. Bring sufficient supply for your trip. For controlled substances, carry the prescription on you at all times. EU Health Insurance Card (EHIC) for EU citizens.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: While not legally required for short stays, strongly recommended. EU citizens should carry the EHIC/GHIC card for state healthcare access.
travelInsurance.tips: For EU citizens, the EHIC provides access to state healthcare at reduced cost. For non-EU citizens, travel insurance with comprehensive medical coverage is essential. French hospitals may bill directly or require payment upfront.

recommended: Hepatitis A (for close contact with locals or extended stays)
Tick-borne encephalitis (for rural/forest areas in eastern France)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations (MMR, DTaP, etc.) are up to date.

healthInfo.waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout France. Bottled water (eau minérale) is widely available if preferred.
healthInfo.foodSafetyTips: France has excellent food safety standards. Cheese, raw milk products, and undercooked meats are popular — these are generally safe but may cause stomach upset if you're not used to them.oysters and shellfish are popular but should be from reputable sources. Wild mushroom foraging is dangerous — only eat mushrooms from trusted sources.
healthInfo.medicalTourismNote: France is a destination for cosmetic surgery and luxury medical retreats. High-quality care at moderate costs compared to the US.

emergency.notes: SAMU (15) for medical, Pompiers (18) for fire also handles medical. 112 works everywhere.

healthcare.costForTourists: Excellent quality, often ranked #1 globally. GP visit €25-50. ER visit €100-300. Tourists pay upfront and claim back with travel insurance. EU citizens use EHIC.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies marked with green cross are everywhere. French pharmacists are highly trained — they can diagnose minor conditions and recommend treatment. Open late and on Sundays on rotation.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: French hospitals are world-class. English-speaking staff available at major Paris hospitals (Hôpital Américain de Paris, Hôpital Européen Georges-Pompidou). Outside Paris, English may be limited.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance recommended. France has reciprocal agreements with many countries. EU citizens use EHIC for public healthcare.

controlledSubstances.note: Now prescription-only in France since 2017 (was previously OTC). Bring your own supply with prescription.

medications.generalAdvice: French pharmacies are excellent. Bring prescriptions in generic/international names — French pharmacists can often provide equivalents. Most common medications available.

scams.name: Gold ring scam
scams.description: Someone 'finds' a gold ring near you and offers it as a gift, then asks for money as a 'finder's fee.' The ring is worthless brass.
scams.avoidance: Ignore anyone who 'finds' something near you. Walk away without engaging.

scams.name: Petition clipboard scam
scams.description: Groups of young people ask you to sign a petition for deaf/mute charity. While you're distracted signing, an accomplice pickpockets you. Or they demand a 'donation' after signing.
scams.avoidance: Don't stop for petition-holders near tourist sites. Say 'Non merci' and keep walking.

scams.name: Three-card Monte / shell game
scams.description: Street gambling game where 'plants' in the audience appear to win big. You cannot win — it's sleight of hand. The crowd may include pickpockets.
scams.avoidance: Never engage with street gambling. Don't even stop to watch — it makes you a pickpocket target.

scams.name: Bracelet sellers at Sacré-Cœur
scams.description: Men aggressively tie string bracelets on your wrist at the steps of Sacré-Cœur and demand €5-10. They may grab your arm.
scams.avoidance: Keep hands in pockets on the Sacré-Cœur steps. Firmly refuse and don't let anyone touch your hands.

connectivity.simOptions: Orange, SFR, or Free Mobile SIM at airports, tabac shops, or Free stores. €10-20 for 30 days with 20-100GB. eSIM via Airalo €5-10. Free Mobile offers excellent value.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most cafes, restaurants, and public spaces. Paris has free WiFi in parks and public buildings. Generally reliable.
connectivity.bestOption: Free Mobile SIM (best value) or Orange (best coverage). eSIM if your phone supports it.

cultural.tipping: Service charge (service compris) is included in all restaurant bills by law. Round up or leave €1-2 for great service. No obligation to tip beyond this.
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual in Paris — jeans are fine but not athletic wear or flip-flops. Cover shoulders at churches. Parisians dress well; you'll stand out in shorts and sneakers.
cultural.greetings: La bise — cheek kiss greeting (2 in Paris, 3 or 4 in some regions). Handshake in formal settings. Always say 'Bonjour' when entering a shop — it's considered rude not to.
taboos: Speaking loudly in restaurants or on public transit
Not greeting shopkeepers with 'Bonjour' before asking anything
Assuming everyone speaks English without first trying French
cultural.haggling: Not practiced except at flea markets (marchés aux puces). Prices are fixed everywhere else.

safety.lgbtSafety: Same-sex marriage legal since 2013. Very tolerant in cities. Paris has one of the largest LGBTQ+ communities in Europe (Le Marais district). Rural areas can be more conservative.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Generally safe. Some catcalling, especially in northern Paris suburbs. Avoid RER B late at night. Tourist areas are well-policed.
safety.notes: France is safe for tourists. Main risks are pickpocketing in Paris (metro, tourist sites) and occasional strikes that disrupt transportation. Avoid protests/demonstrations — they can turn confrontational.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free in Schengen area. UK: 90 days. EU: unlimited.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-June and September-October. Paris is lovely in spring. August many Parisians leave and some shops close. Winter is cold but atmospheric.
